Outline: 

- Why Ensemble?
- Decision Trees

--- 

Up to this point, we have introduced a variety of tools for classification
and regression. In the regression context, we took `OLS` as our basic model
and extended it in a variety of ways: 

- We first derived OLS as the MSE-ERM among linear predictors, showing that
  OLS is 'right' for any problem where we want to predict a mean, even if
  there are no Gaussian assumptions in sight.
- Analyzing the MSE loss, we found our _bias-variance_ decomposition, showing
  that we could break down test error into a sum of distinct components. 
- Ridge and Lasso regularization allowed us to control the size of the
  regression coefficients in either a 'Euclidean' or 'Taxicab' way.
  - By keeping regression coefficients small, these techniques allow us to
    fit models even in the $p \gg n$ setting. (Among the infinite number of
    possible solutions, all with equal training error, regularization picks
    out the 'smallest' one)
  - Ridge regression provides a essentially-guaranteed (small) out-of-sample
    prediction boost using 'shrinkage' to trade off a large variance decrease
    for a small bias increase. While we set up regression as a particular
    $\ell_2^2$ penalty, we saw that _many_ techniques in ML have the same
    effect. Ridge regression, at least, has an explicit _bias-variance_ 
    **tradeoff**, not just a decomposition. 
  - Lasso regression provides a different form of shrinkage and allows us to
    automatically force some components all the way to zero, achieving an
    automated model selection process. 
- Moving beyond linearity, we saw how (polynomial) feature expansion could
  be used to get a better approximation to the underlying relationship, at
  the cost of increased statistical instability (variance). 
  
  - To counteract this increase in variance, we used a variety of techniques:
  
    - Local polynomials, that allow us to use a lower degree polynomial to
      fit a smaller region of the data at a time
    - Spline models that allow us to smoothly switch between local models
      instead of 'going wild' with high powers
    - Ridge regression to ensure our higher degree terms don't inflate our
      variance
    - _Additive_ models allow for 'coordinate-wise' non-linearity and provide
      an attractive middle-ground between linear models and full nonlinearity
      
- To move from regression to classification, we first detoured through
  _generalized_ linear models, which replace the normal sampling distribution
  with a different distribution on $Y$. 
  
  - To predict $Y$, these models target $\E[Y|X] = f(X\beta)$ where $f(\cdot)$
    is some function that maps the unbounded range of $X\beta$ to the
    appropriate mean of $Y$.
  - Important examples: logistic regression (Bernoulli with sigmoid link),
    log-linear (Poisson with exponential link)
  - To push these even further, we saw that the $X\beta$ term could be
    replaced with essentially any non-linear model (especially additive)
    to provide non-linear classification or count regression
- Other important classification families: 
  - Discriminative methods, which attempt to directly determine the class
    boundaries: logistic regression, SVMs (margin classifiers), neural
    networks (generally)
  - Generative methods, which model $X$ depending on $Y$ and then invert this
    model using Bayes' Rule to build a classifie: NB, LDA, QDA
- The central _motif_ of all of our analysis was the Scylla-and-Charybdis
  of bias and variance. We principally worry about variance, which we tame
  by using simpler (less 'complex') models or larger data sets; when we have
  enough data to make variance a (relative) non-issue, we focus on reducing
  bias by using non-linear methods
  
  This complexity calculus re-appeared throughout our work, informing our
  discussion of hyperparameter selection, different model families, hold-out
  sets, model calibration, *etc.*
  
While this journey has gone _many_ places, we never quite stepped away from one
of our earliest assumptions: 

$$\hat{f} = \argmin_{f \in \Fcal} \text{TrainingError}(f) + \lambda *  \text{Regularization}(f) \tag{R-ERM/SRM}$$

Building on this ERM paradigm, we have always looked for _the_
(singular) best fitting model. While we sometimes 'slanted' away from pure
training error minimization, we still took it for granted that there was
_one_ model we would use. Today, we begin to relax that assumption. 

The study of using _multiple_ models together in a smart way is called 
_ensemble learning_. 

## Ensemble Learning

Ensemble learning relies on the idea that multiple models, smartly combined,
can do better (on average) than any single model. We can divide ensemble
learning into two broad schools: 

- (Weighted) Combination of Models: in these models, we use a weighted
  average (or similar) of models in hopes of a 'wisdom of the crowds'
  phenomenon. We know that we can't guarantee one model to always beat
  another, but we hope that by taking an average, the errors of each 
  model will average out and we'll wind up somewhere better than any
  individual input model.
  
  I like to think of these ensemble strategies as _parallel_. We fit 
  many models 'unaware' of each other and then combine them _ex post_. 
  
- Repeated improvement: given one model, we know when it gets the right
  answer and when it makes mistakes (at least on our training data). 
  Is it possible to fit a new model that doesn't attempt to predict $Y$
  directly, but instead targets $Y - f(X) = Y - \hat{Y}$. This model 
  serves as a 'corrective' to the original model and (hopefully) improves
  its performance. We repeat this process again and again (correcting
  the corrected corrections...) until we have a very powerful ensemble. 
  
  These strategies are inhernetly _sequential_: we can't build the
  corrector until the original model has been fitted and tested. 
  
Let's begin by focusing on our _parallel_ strategies: before we work out
details, let's pause to think about what situations (if any) we might
expect a sort of weighted average to help us out. 

For simplicity, we'll focus on MSE-loss in the regression setting, though
there's nothing regression specific to the techniques we're going to look
at. 


Suppose that we want to predict the outcome of some variable $Y$ using
two *statistically independent* predictors $\hat{Y}_1, \hat{Y}_2$: if
*arguendo* we assume these are unbiased, the MSE of each prediction
is simply

$$\begin{align*}
\MSE_{\hat{Y}_i} &= \E_{Y, \hat{Y}_i}[(Y - \hat{Y}_i)^2] \\
                       &= \E_{Y, \hat{Y}_i}[(Y - \E[Y] + \E[Y] - \hat{Y}_i)^2] \\
                       &= \E_{Y, \hat{Y}_i}[(Y - \E[Y])^2 +2(Y - \E[Y])(\E[Y] - \hat{Y}_i)+(\E[Y] - \hat{Y}_i)^2] \\
                       &= \E_{Y}[(Y - \E[Y])^2 +2\E_{Y, \hat{Y}_i}[(Y - \E[Y])(\E[Y] - \hat{Y}_i)]+\E_{\hat{Y}_i}[(\E[Y] - \hat{Y}_i)^2] \\
                       &= \sigma_Y^2 + 2\E_{Y}[Y - \E[Y]]\E_{\hat{Y}_i}[\E[Y] - \hat{Y}_i)] + \sigma^2_{\hat{Y}_i} \\
                       &= \sigma_Y^2 + \sigma^2_{\hat{Y}_i}
\end{align*}$$

(Why do the cross terms vanish?) That is, the MSE is simply sum of the 
'irreducible error' associated with the best possible prediction ($\sigma_Y^2$
against the optimal prediction $\E[Y]$) and the variance (error) in $\hat{Y}_i$
as an estimator of $\E[Y]$.

If $\hat{Y}_1, \hat{Y}_2$ are both predictors of $Y$, it is natural to ask
if we can do better using a *combination* of the two of them than we can with
either separately. Indeed, if we let $\widehat{Y} = \frac{1}{2}(\hat{Y}_1 + \hat{Y}_2)$, the above analysis tells us: 

$$\begin{align*}
\MSE_{\widehat{Y}} &= \sigma_Y^2 + \sigma_{\widehat{Y}}^2 \\
&= \sigma_Y^2 + \V\left[\frac{\hat{Y}_1 + \hat{Y}_2}{2}\right] \\
&= \sigma_Y^2 + \sigma_{\hat{Y}_1}^2/4 + \sigma_{\hat{Y}_2}^2/4
\end{align*}$$

How does this compare to the separate predictions? Well, if 
$\sigma_{\hat{Y}_1} = \sigma_{\hat{Y}_2}$, then we have clearly reduced our 
expected MSE by half of the variance error. (By definition, we can't do anything
about the irreducible error.) If, on the other hand, one predictor is much
better than the other, say $\sigma_{\hat{Y}_1}^2 = 400 \sigma_{\hat{Y}_2}^2$,
then we have

$$\begin{align*}
\MSE_{\hat{Y}_1} &= \sigma_Y^2 + 400 \sigma_{\hat{Y}_2}^2 \\
\MSE_{\hat{Y}_2} &= \sigma_Y^2 + \sigma_{\hat{Y}_2}^2 \\
\MSE_{\widehat{Y}} &= \sigma_Y^2 + 100.25 \sigma_{\hat{Y}_2}^2 \\
\end{align*}$$

So we don't beat the superior predictor ($Y_2$), but we comfortably beat the
inferior predictor ($Y_1$). Notably, if we didn't know which predictor
was better and had to select randomly (50/50), we would have an expected
MSE of $\sigma_Y^2 + 200\sigma_{\hat{Y}_2}^2$, so the 'averaging' predictor
is still better. More generally, if $\hat{Y_1}$ is sometimes better and
$\hat{Y_2}$ is better at other times, a suitable averaging strategy will 
do better  *in the long run* than using a single predictor. (We should pick
the averaging weights as a function of the variance of the two approaches and
the relatively frequencies of the $\hat{Y}_1$-better and $\hat{Y}_2$-better
scenarios.)

This example - simple as it is - gets at the core insight of stacking: if we
have several 'good enough' models, we can do better - sometimes much better -
by using a combination of them. This is not guaranteed - if $\hat{Y}_2$ is 
always the 'lower variance' model, adding in some $\hat{Y}_1$ pretty much
always hurts - but we do not expect to have a single 'dominant' model. 
(See earlier discussion of the *No Free Lunch* Theorem.) In 
practice, we typically find ourselves armed with models of similar-enough
performance (logistic regression, linear SVMs, RBF Kernel SVMs, RBF Kernel 
logistic regression) and find that different models perform better on different
inputs. *E.g.*, the 'linear' models might do well far from the decision boundary,
while the 'kernelized' models might improve performance near the decision
boundary while suffering from extra 'wiggliness' (variance) far from the 
decision boundary. 

So what can we take away from this discussion? 

> Low correlation among predictors is helpful. If our base learners give
  the exact same predictions at every point, there's nothing to be gained by 
  combining and comparing them. 

Put another way, ensemble learning benefits from a *diverse* set of base 
learners. We hope to 'combine strength' from different approaches to build
an ensemble predictor that is better than any of its individual components.

The three major ensembling techniques we will cover - stacking, bagging, and 
boosting - essentially come down to different ways of getting this diversity.

The hope of ensemble learning is that by combining several _simple, but
flexible_ base learners we can achieve performance beyond that of any model. 
Because a (linear) average of linear models is still linear, we might hope
that ensemble learning is at its best in situations where our base learners 
are: 

- Quite flexible (non-linear)
- Easily made 'diverse'

and that we don't really need to worry about variance all that much. This
suggests it is time to introduce the final _base learner_ of this unit, the
humble *decision tree*.

## Decision Trees

You are almost certainly already familiar with 
decision trees through diagrams like this: 

```{r}
#| echo: true
library(rpart)
library(rpart.plot)
library(MASS)
dtree <- rpart(medv ~ . , data=Boston)

rpart.plot(dtree)
```

Here, the tree is evaluated by applying a series of _univariate[^ob] binary_
decision rules 'downwards': that is, at each step, we ask one step about
one variable and take the left or right branch as appropriate. The final
terminus (or 'leaf') of the tree is then our prediction.

[^ob]: This model can be generalized to decisions like $3x_1 + 2x_2 < 5$ instead
of simple univariate rules like $x_1 < 2.5$. These sorts of trees, often called
*oblique* trees because they have decision boundaries that are not axis-aligned,
are rather more difficult computationally, so you won't see them used as much,
but they are popular among theory-minded researchers. 

Decision trees are incredibly popular because they are easy to apply
'mentally' and suggest natural interpretations. Variables which are
used to split early or split often are more important. Interestingly, 
decision trees also can be used to give an 'intermediate prediction'
which is what we would get by stopping the prediction at that point. 
Splits which materially change the intermediate prediction are 
also more important. 

But how should we *actually fit* a decision tree to data? This is, like
so much in machine learning, the sort of thing which is easy to 
understand intuitively, but comes with a significant amount of bookkeeping
in practice. 

Essentially, trees are fit by repeatedly asking the question: "What split
would most reduce the error if my predictions stop here?" So, for the 
first split, the tree looks at each variable to determine its optimal
split point, and then finds the optimal variable to split on. To find
the optimal split point, we need to sort the data on that variable
and then compute the 'before' and 'after' variance for each value. 
After finding the first split, the two 'second level' splits repeat
this process _on only the data in their path_. That is, the two 'second
level' splits are found on _different_ data. The four 'third level' splits
are found on four different data sets, *etc.* 

Because the later splits are computed on different data sets, they 
almost always select different variables at each level (as in our
example above, where the two 'level two' splits use the `lstat` and `rm`
variables). Predictions are made by taking the average (or majority)
of data left in that split. 

Note that the splits need not be _and typically are not_ 'even' splits
along a variable. *E.g.*, if we were doing a split on a variable that
looks like

| Variable | Value | 
|----------|-------|
| 1.0      | 1.0   | 
| 1.1      | 0.9   | 
| 1.2      | 1.1   | 
| 1.3      | 1.4   | 
| 100      | 500   | 
| 105      | 550   | 

The optimal split is clearly something like $\texttt{Variable} \leq 1.3$ with
conditional predictions of $1.1$ and $525$ in each split and split sizes
of $4$ and $2$. 

Clearly, if the tree is allowed to run 'to completion', there will be
one data point left in each leaf and the tree can obtain 0 training error. 
That is, maximal decision trees are a very high complexity (low bias, 
high variance) model. On the other extreme, a 'single split' tree (often
called a 'stump') will be low complexity (high bias, low variance). So
we can take tree depth (number of levels) as a good proxy for model
complexity. Like $K$-Nearest Neighbors, we can pick depth (complexity)
by a suitable cross-validation or train-test scheme, but will soon see
a better way. 

Some other notes on trees: 

- You will sometimes see decision trees refered to as `CART`
  (Classification and Regression Trees) or `rpart` (Recursive Partitioning)
  but most folks will know the term "decision trees" so I just use that. 
- Trees extend _very naturally_ to categorical variables and do not require
  numeric encoding: we simply have to adapt the decision rule from 
  $x \leq y$ to $x \in \Ycal$ where $x$ is now a categorical feature
  and $\Ycal$ is a set of lables. 
- Trees also handle missing values nicely: we can simply treat `NA` as
  _very high_ or _very low_ or use an explicit `is.na` decision rule
- Trees are rather robust to outliers: if a data point has an extreme
  value, it will be 'split away' rather early and the 'main branch' of
  the tree will be fit on the rest of the data. Non-outlier test points
  will funnel into this 'main branch' and it will be like the outlier
  essentially never existed
  
There are tons of tiny little decisions in building trees, so I don't
recommend writing your own implementation. See, *e.g.*, `?rpart.control`
for the fitting parameters used by the `rpart` package: other software
will have similar options. 

## Trees as Ensemble Base Learners

Decision trees represent a nearly-perfect input to a model ensemble: they are
quick to fit, easily modified to achieve all sorts of one-off-rules and are
quite low bias (when deep). It's worth taking a moment to see what that 
low bias looks like. 

Here, I'm going to fit a series of decision trees of increasing depth to a 
(one dimensional) non-linear example.

```{r}
#| echo: false
library(rpart)
library(tidyverse)
library(glue)

f <- function(x) 2 * x + sin(x^3) + 5 * sqrt(log(x^2+1))
tibble(x=seq(-3, 3, length.out=201)) |> 
    mutate(y=f(x), 
           y_depth1 = predict(rpart(y ~ x, control=rpart.control(maxdepth=1, 
                                                                 minbucket=1, 
                                                                 minsplit=1, 
                                                                 cp=0))), 
           y_depth2 = predict(rpart(y ~ x, control=rpart.control(maxdepth=2, 
                                                                 minbucket=1, 
                                                                 minsplit=1, 
                                                                 cp=0))), 
           y_depth3 = predict(rpart(y ~ x, control=rpart.control(maxdepth=3, 
                                                                 minbucket=1, 
                                                                 minsplit=1, 
                                                                 cp=0))), 
           y_depth4 = predict(rpart(y ~ x, control=rpart.control(maxdepth=4, 
                                                                 minbucket=1, 
                                                                 minsplit=1, 
                                                                 cp=0))), 
           y_depth5 = predict(rpart(y ~ x, control=rpart.control(maxdepth=5, 
                                                                 minbucket=1, 
                                                                 minsplit=1, 
                                                                 cp=0))),
           y_depth6 = predict(rpart(y ~ x, control=rpart.control(maxdepth=6, 
                                                                 minbucket=1, 
                                                                 minsplit=1, 
                                                                 cp=0)))) |>
    pivot_longer(starts_with("y_"), names_to="model", values_to="y_hat") |>
    mutate(model=glue("Tree Fit: Max Depth {str_sub(model, 8, 8)}")) |>
    ggplot(aes(x=x)) + 
    geom_line(aes(y=y), linewidth=1) + 
    geom_line(aes(y=y_hat), color="blue2", lwd=1.2) + 
    facet_wrap(~model) + 
    theme_bw() 
```

Not surprisingly, as we allow a more complex tree, we are able to fit this
funny shape more and more effectively. Because we have fit a _binary_ tree, 
note the number of 'levels' (leaves) in the final tree: 

- At a depth of 1, we have $2^1=2$ distinct 'chunks' in our fitted estimate
- At a depth of 2, we have $2^2=4$ distinct 'chunks'
- At a depth of 3, we have $2^3=8$ distinct 'chunks'

and so on. Clearly, our function has the potential to become quite complex
(and potentially overfit) quite quickly. 

We see something similar in 2D: 

```{r}
#| echo: false
#| fig-height: 12
library(tidyverse)
library(rpart)

f2d <- function(x1, x2) {
    sin(x1 * 2) + cos(x2 * 2) + 0.5 * (x1^2 - x2^2)
}

grid <- expand_grid(
    x1 = seq(-3, 3, length.out = 201),
    x2 = seq(-3, 3, length.out = 201)
) |> 
    mutate(y = f2d(x1, x2))

depths <- 1:9

fit_depth <- function(d, data) {
    model <- rpart(
        y ~ x1 + x2,
        data = data,
        control = rpart.control(
            maxdepth  = d,
            cp        = 0,
            minsplit  = 2,
            minbucket = 1
        )
    )
    predict(model, newdata = data)
}

tree_preds <- map(depths, \(d) {
    grid |> 
        mutate(
            val = fit_depth(d, grid),
            panel = sprintf("Tree Depth %d", d)
        )
}) |> 
    bind_rows()

bind_rows(
    grid |> mutate(val = y, panel = "True Function"),
    tree_preds)|> 
    mutate(panel = factor(panel, 
                          levels = c("True Function", 
                                     sprintf("Tree Depth %d", depths)))) |>
    ggplot(aes(x = x1, y = x2)) +
    geom_raster(aes(fill=val), 
                interpolate = FALSE) +
    geom_contour(aes(z = val), color = "black", alpha = 0.25, bins = 8) +
    facet_wrap(~ panel, ncol=2) +
    scale_fill_distiller(name = expression(hat(y)), type="div", palette=6) +
    coord_fixed() +
    theme_bw() +
    theme(
        strip.text = element_text(face = "bold", size = 10),
        legend.position = "bottom"
    ) +
    labs(
        title = "2D Trees: Effect of Maximum Tree Depth",
        subtitle = "Piecewise-constant orthogonal partitions approximating a smooth surface",
        x = expression(x[1]),
        y = expression(x[2])
    ) 
```

Here, we see that instead of getting 1D steps, we have a 2D 
[Mondrian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Piet_Mondrian) structure to
our predictions.[^plaid] Beyond the increasing complexity, there are a few
interesting things to notice: 

- Like our 1D example, we still have _piecewise constant_ predictions.
- Our partitions (breaks) are axis-aligned (sometimes called 'orthogonal')
  because we only split on one variable at a time. (_Oblique_ trees could allow
  diagonal splits, but we won't really dig into those in this course.)
  
These will generally hold for arbitrary numbers of predictors. As with our
one-dimensional case, the number of partitions still grows as $2^{\text{depth}}$.

[^plaid]: Sometimes, this might be described as a _plaid_ pattern, but
that's almost certainly wrong. Plaids are quite regularly spaced; trees, as we
see here, can be quite flexible.

From the above, it's easy to see that very deep trees can easily overfit, but we 
want to at least consider the possibility of high depth if our data demands it.
(This should remind you of the general role of regularization.) So, other than 
using very simple trees, what other tools and techniques can we
use to control the complexity of the fitted model? 

*(In the examples above, I turned off all of the other 'complexity control' knobs
but now we're going to start turning them back on.)*

As with $1$-NN, we know that things can get _very_ complex when we only look at
one observation (or a small number of observations) to make a prediction, so 
we might want to early stop our trees. In particular, we can add rules that say: 

- Don't split a node that currently has less than $n_{\text{min-split}}$ 
  observations in it. This doesn't stop the tree from continuing to grow, but
  it forces the algorithm to look elsewhere, rather than to continue further and
  further subdividing that part of the space.
- Don't split a node if it produces _significantly_ imbalance splits. If we have
  a node with 100 observations, we may be willing to split it, but not in a
  99-vs-1 way. Instead of getting the 'optimal' split, we can restrict ourselves
  to splits that leave at least $n_{\text{min-bucket}}$ observations in the
  resulting nodes. 
  
  These are quite similar and easily confused: the `min-split` is a constraint 
  on the _parent_, considered _before_ splitting; `min-bucket` is a constraint 
  on the _children_, considered _after_ forming a split. In practice, you
  will typically only set one or the other of these. (I have seen `min-split`
  used more often since it's a bit faster and easier to implement.)
- We can also take an idea from model selection, where we only include a variable
  if it 'proves its worth'. In the tree context, we might include a split only
  if it lowers our training error by a sufficient amount. Instead of hard-capping
  the tree in various ways, this has a smoother, more adaptive, feel. 
  
  Depending on the particular set-up, there are different loss functions you 
  might look at (change in MSE, change in $R^2$, change in classification accuracy), 
  but the general idea of "only if it's worth it" can be applied similarly (modulo
  some changes in units).
